            if notes != exp: fails.append(f"{slot}: notes differ {sorted(set(exp)^set(notes))}")

    if m["state"] in ("partial","notes-only"):

for c in snap["lr_answer_choices"]:

    if not n or n["choice_text"] != c["choice_text"] or n["is_correct"] != c["is_correct"]: fails.append(f"choice {c['id']} changed")
# other explanation rows in snapshot untouched
for s in snap["lr_explanation_steps"]:
    pass
print("slot failures:", fails or "none")
# DB-side completeness: a question is complete if some single/standard explanation has >=1 step and notes A-E
def complete(qid_):

        if e["style"] in ("single", "standard") and st[e["id"]] and sorted({n["letter"] for n in nt[e["id"]]}) == list("ABCDE"):

    return False

for m in man:

## PT102-S3-Q16 | Dispute | C

> Motorcoach driver: Professional drivers spend much more time driving, on average, than do other people and hence are more competent drivers than are other, less experienced drivers. Therefore, the speed limit on major highways should not be reduced, because that action would have the undesirable effect of forcing some people who are now both law-abiding and competent drivers to break the law.

Police officer: All drivers can drive within the legal speed limit if they wish, so it is not true to say that reducing the speed limit would be the cause of such illegal behavior.
>
> The point at issue between the motorcoach driver and the police officer is whether
>
> (A) it would be desirable to reduce the speed limit on major highways
> (B) professional drivers will drive within the legal speed limit if that limit is reduced
> (C) reducing the speed limit on major highways would cause some professional drivers to break the law
> (D) professional drivers are more competent drivers than are other, less experienced drivers
> (E) all drivers wish to drive within the speed limit

### Argument Breakdown

**Motorcoach driver's Position:** Lowering the speed limit would force some competent, law-abiding drivers to break the law, so it should not be lowered.

**Police officer's Position:** Every driver can stay under the limit if they want to, so a lower limit would not *cause* anyone to break the law.

**Evaluate:** The officer answers only one of the driver's claims: that a lower limit would *cause* lawbreaking. The officer says nothing about whether professional drivers are more competent, or whether lowering the limit is a good idea. The clash is on cause.

**Goal:** Whether lowering the speed limit would cause some drivers to break the law.

### Choice Notes

**(A) Half Scope.** This is the most popular wrong answer. The driver clearly thinks lowering the limit is undesirable. But the officer never says whether it is a good idea. They only dispute the "cause" claim, so we cannot support the officer's side here.

**(B) Half Scope.** The officer says drivers *can* stay within the limit, not that they *will*. "Can" and "will" are different claims.

**(C) Correct.** The driver says a lower limit would force lawbreaking. The officer says it would not be the cause. That is the disagreement.

**(D) Half Scope.** The driver says professionals are more competent. The officer does not address competence.

**(E) Out of Scope.** Neither speaker talks about what all drivers *wish*.

- **Scan for the indicator, then ask the two conditional questions out loud.** "Can I chain it? Can I apply it to a fact (usually via the contrapositive)?" appears almost word for word in PT103-S1-Q19 and PT155-S1-Q15, and it drives both the Evaluate and the Goal. When there is a Most claim and a conditional, the best ones say which one commands attention and why (PT145-S2-Q23: a lone Most is inert; PT122-S4-Q19).
- **Rewrite rules into "X requires Y" before chaining.** PT155-S1-Q15, PT140-S3-Q17 and PT148-S3-Q17 turn "unless", "only when", "essential", "cannot until" into requirements, so the chain reads left to right and the contrapositive is easy to state in plain English.
- **The Goal names the answer's content and its strength.** Strong: "look for something like 'the symptoms relate to collagen'" (PT153-S2-Q5); "Pulham has to be higher than 38%" (PT155-S4-Q21); "an answer expressing this stalemate" (PT148-S3-Q17). The better ones also predict where the traps will go ("expect illegal negations and reversals", PT140-S3-Q17; the list of overconfident directions in PT142-S4-Q11).
- **Pivot endings get a named move and a worked mini-example.** "Reconcile the Pivot" with the Tom/Yankees example (PT142-S4-Q11), and the rebuttal reading plus "Flip the Causal Difference-Maker" (PT151-S3-Q14). Both warn that the right answer will be watered down.
- **Quantity inferences are taught with head counts, not only symbols.** PT148-S1-Q22 (15 ballet lovers, minimum 17 cake lovers), PT145-S2-Q23 (100 Velyena mines vs 11 gold mines), PT155-S4-Q21 (100 + 100 students, 47%). The rule is stated so it can be memorized ("Most A are B, Most B are not A: more B than A"), then the numbers make it believable.
- **Weak wording is argued for, not just noticed.** The best correct notes say how little evidence the answer needs: "no guarantee" needs one data point (PT102-S4-Q2, the 175/UCLA example); "sometimes" needs one case (PT151-S3-Q14, PT108-S2-Q17); "can be altered" (PT107-S1-Q6).
- **Recurring trap names, each with a one-line test.** One-claim answer ("feels like the first sentence on steroids", PT148-S3-Q17; PT147-S4-Q23 C); relative vs absolute (PT107-S1-Q6 A, PT140-S3-Q17 B); only mentioned ≠ only (PT103-S1-Q19); unknown Most group ("never conclude Most X without a Most X premise", PT145-S2-Q23); untriggered rule ("we don't have any knowledge triggered by...", PT155-S1-Q15, PT149-S4-Q24).
- **The popular trap gets the longest note and a counterexample.** PT122-S4-Q19 B (30%), PT140-S3-Q17 A and B (21% and 23%), PT146-S2-Q17 C (29%), PT148-S1-Q22 C (19%) each build a concrete scenario where the premises are true and the trap is false.
- **When the key is not strictly provable, they say so and say why it still wins.** PT155-S1-Q15 (allowed outside vs outside), PT107-S1-Q6 (volume dial is not causal, but the stimulus supports it), PT142-S4-Q7 (correlation to "reasonable to conclude"). That honesty is part of teaching Most Supported.
- **Reusable phrases:** "pause and infer"; "X requires Y"; "remove the overlap and join the one-offs"; "we don't have any knowledge triggered by X"; "if it said ___, it would be correct" (PT149-S4-Q24 E); "this is the first sentence on steroids".

### What the weaker MBT candidates got wrong

- **Goal hands off to the answers.** PT149-S3-Q21 ("re-read the paragraph ... then use the answers to guide us"), PT146-S2-Q17 and PT147-S4-Q23 admit they cannot predict. Acceptable when the stimulus is a scatter, but it costs P every time.
- **Pasted notes instead of question-specific reasons.** PT154-S2-Q22 repeats the same Most rule in B, C and E, and C borrows B's closing sentence, which does not address oil paintings. PT127-S1-Q17 gives D (22%) and E the same one-line note. PT107-S4-Q23 pastes the one-claim paragraph into B and C.
- **Unsupported test-taking folklore.** PT149-S3-Q21 and PT107-S1-Q21 both claim the tempting wrong answer is deliberately placed in slot (A). That is not a reasoning move and should not be copied.
- **Diagrams flattened into unreadable lines.** PT111-S3-Q18 and PT108-S3-Q23 are strong underneath, but the conditional chains now read as word salad ("inspired → good → sophistic → underst performances show listeners m. roots").
- **The popular trap gets the shortest note.** PT127-S1-Q17 D (22%): one line pasted from E. PT145-S4-Q13: A, B, C are one line each and E defers to "the explanation for (C)".

### What the best MBF explanations do

- **Open Evaluate with the two-pattern rule, then look for each.** "The correct answer almost always contradicts a conditional or contradicts an inference we can make by combining claims" (PT127-S1-Q25, PT113-S3-Q15, PT147-S1-Q20). Then they actually derive the inference or state the contradiction shape, rather than stopping at the rule.
- **Define a contradiction precisely and separate it from a bad inference.** "Trigger, but don't deliver" (PT153-S3-Q16); "a contradiction provides the trigger but denies the outcome; reversals and negations are illegal but not contradictions" (PT115-S2-Q24); "Bad Inference ≠ contradiction" (PT124-S2-Q10). This is the single most important transfer line for the family.
- **Every wrong-answer note runs the same test: what would we need to have read to contradict this?** PT110-S3-Q22, PT121-S4-Q18, PT148-S1-Q10 and PT122-S2-Q21 phrase it as "To contradict this, we would need to have read that ___. We never heard that." PT113-S3-Q15 and PT117-S4-Q18 phrase it as "Can I prove the opposite?" Either way, it replaces verdict-only "out of scope" notes.
- **Teach the strength asymmetry.** Weak claims ("some", "commonly", "could") are hard to contradict; strong claims ("no", "never", "invariably", "no techniques") fall to one counterexample. PT110-S3-Q22 states it, PT149-S3-Q12 and PT148-S1-Q10 apply it to soft stems, PT122-S2-Q21 applies it to a causal passage.
- **Predict the disguise.** PT153-S3-Q16 predicts filler around the trigger ("hates pasta"); PT147-S1-Q20 says D matches the prediction "but they disguised it well"; PT142-S4-Q23 predicts two requirements in tension before reading the choices.
- **Locate answers by position on a chain.** PT115-S2-Q24: "something is the 1st idea but not the 3rd" contradicts; "the 4th but not the 3rd" does not. That turns five choices into one quick check.
- **Run numbers on quantified "or" and Most claims.** PT127-S1-Q25 (30% + 30% non-overlapping; 49% + 2%) and PT113-S3-Q15 ($1 million at 20% vs 13%) make the math visible, and PT127-S1-Q25's NFL/Mars example shows why a Most "or" claim can be satisfied by one side alone.
- **Tell the student what one word would make a wrong answer right.** PT153-S3-Q16 B ("if it said some popular novelists"), PT105-S4-Q21 A. This shows exactly where the line is.
- **Reusable phrases:** "trigger, but don't deliver"; "can't prove it ≠ can disprove it" (PT102-S4-Q15); "we can't contradict something we never talked about"; "to contradict this, we would need to know ___"; "could I infer that the opposite must be true?".

### What the weaker MBF candidates got wrong

- **Verdict-only notes, especially for "out of scope" answers.** PT134-S2-Q18 (notes of one sentence each), PT129-S2-Q23, PT102-S4-Q15 (A to D are one or two lines). An out-of-scope note is only useful when it says what contradiction would have been needed.
- **Pasted notes.** PT152-S2-Q24 D and E are identical (and both wrong, below); PT122-S2-Q16 B, C, E share one note; PT105-S4-Q21 D and E share one note; PT108-S3-Q18 opens A, B, C, E with the same boilerplate.
- **Slips that invert the logic of a note.** PT152-S2-Q24 says "we can contradict this" where it means "can't"; PT116-S3-Q17's Goal lists a wrong second contradiction pattern; PT122-S4-Q5's Evaluate treats a Most claim as All. In a family built on the difference between can't-prove and can-disprove, these are serious.
- **Popular trap under-served.** PT102-S4-Q16 B (39%) gets two sentences; PT147-S1-Q20 E (17%) and PT102-S4-Q26 A (16%) get one line.
- **Different register.** PT112-S4-Q7 uses heavy em-dashes and a voice unlike the rest of the corpus ("i.e., which answer is ruled out"); accurate, but not a style model.

"""Validate a batch of LR explanation drafts (usage: generate_batch_sql.py NN [bank_dir]) and emit guarded insert-only SQL, one transaction per slot. No database writes.

Handles four slot states:
  unloaded     question absent: insert question + choices (bank text) + explanation
  unexplained  question present, no single/standard explanation: insert explanation
  notes-only   explanation has steps but no notes: insert five notes
  partial      explanation has steps and some notes: insert only the missing letters
"""

import sys
from pathlib import Path
sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]))
from project_paths import project_path
import json
import re
from collections import defaultdict

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[3]
BATCH = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "02"
DRAFTS = sorted((ROOT / "corpus/lr-explanations/drafts").glob(f"batch-{BATCH}-*-part-*.md"))
DB = ROOT / "system/scripts/lsatlab-pull/data/db"
BANK = Path(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else project_path("lsatu-wt-bankfix-b02", "public", "data")
OUT = ROOT / f"corpus/lr-explanations/work/batch-{BATCH}-inputs"
Q = f"$batch{BATCH}$"
NOTE = f"Batch {BATCH}; question text from local bank."
TYPE_FIX = {"PT147-S4-Q16": "Parallel Flaw", "PT156-S4-Q24": "Parallel Flaw"}
TEXT_FIX = {("PT127-S1-Q4", "questionStem"): ("�", "’")}


def lit(s):
    if Q in s:
        raise ValueError("delimiter in text")
    return f"{Q}{s}{Q}"


def norm_text(s):
    """Collapse hard line wraps inside paragraphs; keep blank-line paragraph breaks."""
    paras = re.split(r"\n\s*\n", s.strip())
    return "\n\n".join(re.sub(r"\s*\n\s*", " ", p).strip() for p in paras)


def records(name):
    return json.loads((DB / f"{name}.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


def parse_drafts():
    slots = {}
    for path in DRAFTS:
        text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        for sec in text.split("\n## ")[1:]:
            head = sec.split("\n", 1)[0]
            slot, qtype, key = [x.strip() for x in head.split("|")]
            steps, notes = [], {}
            bd = sec.split("### Argument Breakdown", 1)
            if len(bd) == 2:
                part = bd[1].split("### Choice Notes", 1)[0]
                for m in re.finditer(r"^\*\*(.+?):\*\* (.+?)(?=\n\n\*\*|\Z)", part.strip(), re.S | re.M):
                    steps.append((m.group(1).strip(), m.group(2).strip()))
            cn = sec.split("### Choice Notes", 1)[1] if "### Choice Notes" in sec else ""
            for m in re.finditer(r"^\*\*\(([A-E])\) (.+?)\.\*\* (.+?)(?=\n\n\*\*\(|\Z)", cn.strip(), re.S | re.M):
                notes[m.group(1)] = (m.group(2).strip(), m.group(3).strip())
            slots[slot] = dict(type=qtype, key=key, steps=steps, notes=notes)
    return slots


def main():
    drafts = parse_drafts()
    bank = {}
    for f in BANK.glob("PT*-S*-LR.json"):
        for b in json.loads(f.read_text(encoding="utf-8")):
            bank[f"{b['practiceTest']}-S{b['sectionNumber']}-Q{b['questionNumber']}"] = b
    qs = {q["qid"]: q for q in records("lr_questions")}
    exq = defaultdict(list)
    for e in records("lr_explanations"):
        if e["style"] in ("single", "standard"):
            exq[e["question_id"]].append(e)
    st = defaultdict(list)
    for s in records("lr_explanation_steps"):
        st[s["explanation_id"]].append(s)
    nt = defaultdict(dict)

            for L in "ABCDE":

                sql.append(f"INSERT INTO lr_answer_choices (question_id, letter, choice_text, tag, is_correct) SELECT q.id, {lit(L)}, {lit(norm_text(b['answerChoices'][L]))}, {lit(tag)}, {'true' if L == b['correctAnswer'] else 'false'} FROM lr_questions q WHERE q.qid={lit(slot)} AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lr_answer_choices c WHERE c.question_id=q.id AND c.letter={lit(L)}) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;")
            target = "e.style='single'"
            new_expl = True
        else:
            exps = exq[q["id"]]
            sql.append(f"DO $guard$ BEGIN IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lr_questions q WHERE q.qid={lit(slot)} AND q.stimulus={lit(q['stimulus'])} AND q.prompt={lit(q['prompt'])} AND q.correct_choice={lit(q['correct_choice'])}) THEN RAISE EXCEPTION 'Question changed: {slot}'; END IF; END $guard$;")
            if q["correct_choice"] != d["key"]:
                errors.append(f"{slot}: DB key differs")
            if not exps:
                state, new_expl, target = "unexplained", True, "e.style='single'"
                sql.append(f"DO $guard$ BEGIN IF (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM lr_explanations e JOIN lr_questions q ON q.id=e.question_id WHERE q.qid={lit(slot)} AND e.style IN ('single','standard')) <> 0 THEN RAISE EXCEPTION 'Explanation row changed: {slot}'; END IF; END $guard$;")
            else:
                if len(exps) != 1:
                    errors.append(f"{slot}: {len(exps)} explanation rows")

                e = exps[0]
                have = sorted(nt[e["id"]])
                new_expl, target = False, f"e.id={lit(e['id'])}"
                missing = [L for L in "ABCDE" if L not in have]
                if sorted(d["notes"]) != missing:
                    errors.append(f"{slot}: draft letters {sorted(d['notes'])} vs missing {missing}")
                if st[e["id"]]:
                    state = "partial" if have else "notes-only"

            sql.append(f"INSERT INTO lr_explanation_steps (explanation_id, position, label, body) SELECT e.id, v.position, v.label, v.body FROM lr_explanations e JOIN lr_questions q ON q.id=e.question_id CROSS JOIN (VALUES {vals}) v(position,label,body) WHERE q.qid={lit(slot)} AND {target} AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lr_explanation_steps s WHERE s.explanation_id=e.id) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;")

Theo attacks exactly that: popular music can do valuable artistic work without reflecting reality. So the clash is the standard Maria is using.\n\n**Goal:** Whether art has to represent reality accurately to be good art.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Too Strong.** Theo says popular music provides consoling fantasies. Theo never denies that popular music exaggerates love; he says it doesn't have to be realistic. So we can't put him on the other side.\n\n**(C) Too Strong.** This is the most popular wrong answer. Theo's view is that popular music isn't supposed to reflect reality, not that all art should \"always\" show reality \"as it could be\". And Maria wants reality as it is, but says nothing about \"as it could be\". Neither position is supported.\n\n**(D) Correct.** Maria calls popular music bad art *because* it fails to represent reality accurately. Theo says it isn't supposed to reflect reality and still performs artistic functions. So Maria says accuracy is needed for good art, and Theo says it isn't.\n\n**(E) Both Agree.** Both treat popular music as art. Maria calls it \"bad art\" and Theo talks about its \"artistic functions\".\n\n## PT118-S1-Q10 | Agree/Disagree | A\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Rachel's Position:** Freedom from old constraints has caused a decline in the quality of art. James says the belief that contemporary art is generally inferior is a mistake. James never discusses Rachel's reason (constraints). He goes after her conclusion.\n\n**Goal:** Whether contemporary art is actually worse than earlier art.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.** Rachel: freedom \"has caused a decline in the quality of art\". James: people \"mistakenly think that contemporary art is generally inferior to earlier art\". Worse versus not worse.\n\n**(B) Half Scope.** This is the most popular wrong answer. Rachel does say today's artists are free of their predecessors' constraints, so she would deny B. But James says nothing about constraints, so we can't place him.\n\n**(C) Half Scope.** Rachel says this almost word for word. Rachel doesn't touch this either.\n\n## PT119-S2-Q1 | Agree/Disagree | D\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Cox's Position:** The council did not give sufficient justification for recalling Derma-35.\n\n**Crockett's Position:** \"I disagree.\" The council cited blemishes, and it was right that blemishes are a legitimate health concern. Channen: some people want the money for goods, \"even if you are indifferent to what others think of you\".\n\n## PT126-S4-Q8 | Agree/Disagree | A\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Larew's Position:** The lowest quintile's average income rose by a much higher percentage than the highest quintile's, so their prosperity rose relative to the highest.\n\n**Mendota's Position:** \"I disagree.\" The percentage may have been bigger, but the dollar increase was surely bigger for the highest quintile.\n\n**Evaluate:** Read Mendota's concession carefully: \"may have increased by a greater percentage\". Mendota isn't disputing the numbers. Mendota disputes what they show. Larew measures relative prosperity by percentage change; Mendota says the absolute dollar change matters. Picture it: 10% of $10,000 is $1,000, and 5% of $200,000 is $10,000. The gap in dollars grew even though the poorer group's percentage was higher.\n\n**Goal:** Whether comparing percentage changes is the right way to measure relative prosperity.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.** Larew moves straight from \"higher percentage increase\" to \"prosperity increased relative\" to the top, so he treats percentages as the right measure. C states the principle directly, so it is the stronger answer.\n\n**(C) Correct.** Sherrie: addictiveness alone justifies restricting tobacco. Fran grants the definition (\"By your own admission\").\n\n**(E) Out of Scope.** Neither speaker talks about scientists cooperating with governments.\n\n## PT128-S2-Q16 | Agree/Disagree | C\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Laurel's Position:** Modern moral theories must be discarded or greatly reworked, because they fail to guide us in extreme cases, when we need guidance most.\n\n**Miriam's Position:** A moral theory, like an overcoat, can be useful without working in every situation. Miriam: being useful in \"a wide variety of common circumstances is all we need\".\n\n**(D) Out of Scope.** This twists the analogy. ## PT104-S1-Q7 | Paradox | C

**Modelled on:** PT148-S3-Q11 (difference between groups), PT140-S1-Q20 (part vs whole).


### Argument Breakdown

**Given that:** Most magazines have lost advertising revenue in the recession, enough to put the most widely read magazines in danger.

**How can it be that:** People are reading more magazines than ever, and more magazines are financially successful than ever?

**Evaluate:** Notice the two groups the stimulus names. The danger is to the *most widely read* magazines. The success is counted across magazines in general. If smaller magazines do not depend much on advertising, an ad slump would hurt the big ones while the rest thrive on more readers. Look for something that separates how the two kinds of magazine make money.

**Goal:** Find a difference in revenue source between the most widely read magazines and the others.

### Choice Notes

**(A) Half Scope.** Cheaper ad rates would explain the fall in ad revenue. They do nothing to explain why more magazines than ever are succeeding.

**(B) Out of Scope.** Television audiences do not tell us anything about magazine revenue or magazine success.

**(C) Correct.** Only the biggest magazines live on advertising, so the ad slump threatens them. Everyone else lives on circulation, and more people are reading, so more of them succeed. Both halves of the stimulus now fit.

**(D) Deepens Paradox.** If readers cut subscriptions and borrow copies, circulation revenue falls too. That makes the record number of successful magazines even harder to explain.

**(E) Restates Paradox.** New magazines surviving is one more sign of success. It repeats the surprising fact instead of explaining it.

Tags: Correct, Too Strong, Unsupported, Unsupported Comparison, Opposite, Out of Scope, Reversed.\n\n## PT113-S4-Q1 | Most Supported | C\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** Embezzlers call it \"only borrowing\". The blank asks what follows \"by criminals' characterization\".\n\n**Goal:** In their own telling, what they did wasn't really a crime.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Too Strong.** Saying an act wasn't wrong is not saying it deserves a reward. None of the examples claim credit.\n\n**(B) Unsupported.** This is the most popular wrong answer. \"The victim deserved it\" puts blame on the victim; it doesn't make the criminal a victim of some other criminal. No example says that.\n\n**(C) Correct.** Borrowing, justified, not my fault: each description denies that the act was criminal. That is what all three examples share.\n\n**(D) Out of Scope.** The criminals talk about their own acts, not the justice system.\n\n**(E) Unsupported.** These criminals aren't asking for leniency. They deny there was a crime at all.\n\n## PT113-S4-Q3 | Most Supported | D\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** Same two paintings, same order, two classes. Class one was told painting 1 hung in museums and painting 2 was by an amateur: everyone picked painting 1. Class two was told the reverse: everyone picked painting 2.\n\n**Evaluate:** Pause and infer. The paintings never changed. Only the story changed, and the verdict flipped with it. So what the students were told made a difference to at least some of them.\n\n**Goal:** Some students' judgments were swayed by what they were told about the paintings.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Too Strong.** This is the most popular wrong answer. One comparison against one museum painting tells us nothing about whether students would dislike *any* amateur work.\n\n**(B) Unsupported.** The two classes heard conflicting stories, so some claims were false. But that doesn't mean *none* were true.\n\n**(C) Too Strong.** Preferring one museum painting over one amateur painting says nothing about liking most paintings in any museum.\n\n**(D) Correct.** Same paintings, opposite verdicts, and the only change was the story. \"Some\" is all we need, and the flip gives us that.\n\n**(E) Unsupported.** We have no idea what students would say with no information. Maybe they'd all pick the same one.\n\n## PT114-S2-Q6 | Most Supported | D\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** A representative sample of 1,000 Danish adults: 31% favor a ban on cigarette advertising, 24% oppose it, 38% favor a ban for certain media, 7% have no opinion. Their views barely changed in ten years.\n\n**Evaluate:** Pause and infer with the numbers. 31% want a full ban and 38% want a partial one. That's 69% who want some kind of ban. The sample is representative, so that carries over to the population.\n\n**Goal:** Most Danes favor some sort of ban.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Too Strong.** These people's views changed little on one issue. That says nothing about whether opinions \"never\" change.\n\n**(B) Out of Scope.** The survey doesn't ask about setting a precedent.\n\n**(C) Unsupported.** 93% have an opinion and 69% want a ban. Nothing suggests they aren't concerned.\n\n**(D) Correct.** 31% + 38% = 69% favor a ban of some kind, and the sample represents the population.\n\n**(E) Out of Scope.** The survey is about advertising, not who smokes.\n\n## PT114-S4-Q24 | Most Strongly Supported | E\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** Most land vertebrates have rotating limbs ending in digits, which help on land. Acanthostega was an aquatic animal with a trait that is useful for moving on land. So a characteristic found in an aquatic animal can be an advantage on land. That is exactly the fact the biologists need to \"consider\".\n\n**Goal:** Some traits of water-dwelling animals are useful on land.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Unsupported.** Nothing says land traits are a disadvantage underwater. Acanthostega had them and lived in water.\n\n**(B) Opposite.** Acanthostega is a counterexample: an aquatic animal with a trait useful on land.\n\n**(C) Opposite.** This is the most popular wrong answer. The gills indicate that Acanthostega *and its predecessors* were exclusively aquatic. It didn't start on land.\n\n**(D) Too Strong.** \"All\" characteristics is far beyond one fossil.\n\n**(E) Correct.** Rotating limbs with digits help on land, and Acanthostega, an aquatic animal, had them. \"Certain\" and \"some\" keep it to what the fossil shows.\n\n## PT117-S2-Q2 | Most Supported | E\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** Bypass surgery is commonly done when other therapies would be as effective. The cardiologist compares bypass with \"these other therapies\", not with every alternative there is.\n\n**(B) Unsupported.** Nothing compares today with the past.\n\n**(C) Unsupported.** \"Especially debatable\" for one vessel doesn't mean surgery *should* be done for more than one.\n\n**(D) Unsupported.** The passage says the alternatives are cheaper, not that bypass costs more for single-vessel cases specifically.\n\n**(E) Correct.** \"As effective\" and \"less risk\" come straight from the first two sentences. \"Sometimes\" matches \"commonly performed when\".\n\n## PT117-S3-Q9 | Most Supported | D\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** Rossi: it's undemocratic to live under a government that doesn't represent your interests; children's interests sometimes differ from their parents', so children should vote. And if anything, it would be Naomi, not Ivan, who has the advantage.\n\n**(C) Opposite.** Halle is a third-year, and only fourth-years are guaranteed.\n\n**(D) Correct.** Gerald is a fourth-year on the dean's list; Katrina isn't a fourth-year. Rare threats show up in the news every time; common threats mostly don't. People judge risk by how often they hear about a threat. So people who get their information from the news will see rare threats as bigger, compared with common ones, than they really are.\n\n**Goal:** News-reliant people overestimate rare threats relative to common ones.\n\n## PT126-S4-Q11 | Most Supported | E\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Statements:** Inez: a title should summarize the whole book, and nearly half of *The Nature of Matter* is about energy, so it's mistitled. Antonio's answer is that \"matter\" already covers energy.\n\n**Goal:** Inez thinks the title shouldn't mention matter without also mentioning energy.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Unsupported.** Inez wants a title for the *whole* book. \"The Nature of Energy\" would leave out the other half.\n\n**(B) Too Strong.** \"Two facets of the same phenomenon\" still allows differences between the facets. type RenderableLRQuestionInput = {
  stimulus?: unknown;
  questionStem?: unknown;
  answerChoices?: Partial<Record<'A' | 'B' | 'C' | 'D' | 'E', unknown>>;
};

const sharedPassageMetadataPrefixPattern =
  /^\s*(?:The following passage is used for Section\s+\d+,\s+questions\s+\d+\s+through\s+\d+\.|Questions?\s+\d+\s+(?:through|and|[-–])\s+\d+\s+refer to the following passage\.)\s*/i;
const sharedPassageRangePattern =
  /^\s*(?:The following passage is used for Section\s+\d+,\s+questions\s+(\d+)\s+through\s+(\d+)\.|Questions?\s+(\d+)\s+(?:through|and|[-–])\s+(\d+)\s+refer to the following passage\.)\s*/i;

function stripSharedPassageMetadataPrefix(text: string): string {
  return text.replace(sharedPassageMetadataPrefixPattern, '').trim();
}

function normalizeProseHardWraps(text: string): string {
  return text
    .replace(/\r\n?/g, '\n')
    .split(/\n{2,}/)
    .map((paragraph) => paragraph.replace(/[ \t]*\n[ \t]*/g, ' ').replace(/[ \t]{2,}/g, ' ').trim())
    .filter(Boolean)
    .join('\n\n');
}

function getSharedPassageRange(text: string): { start: number; end: number } | null {
  const match = text.match(sharedPassageRangePattern);
  if (!match) return null;

  const start = Number(match[1] ?? match[3]);
  const end = Number(match[2] ?? match[4]);
  if (!Number.isFinite(start) || !Number.isFinite(end) || start > end) return null;

  return { start, end };
}

const dialogueIntroPattern = /^[A-Z][A-Za-z’' -]{1,80}:\s+/;
const dialogueTransitionPattern = /[.!?]["”')\]]?\s+[A-Z][A-Za-z’' -]{1,80}:\s+/;
// Captures: 1) sentence-ending punctuation, 2) the candidate speaker label
// (without its trailing colon/space), 3) the colon + whitespace that follows.
const dialogueTurnBreakPattern =
  /([.!?]["”')\]]?)\s+([A-Z][A-Za-z’' -]{1,80})(:\s+)/g;

function normalizeDialogueSpeakerBreaks(text: string): string {
  if (!dialogueIntroPattern.test(text) || !dialogueTransitionPattern.test(text)) return text;

  return text.replace(dialogueTurnBreakPattern, (match, punct, label, colon) =>
    looksLikeSpeakerLabel(label) ? `${punct}\n\n${label}${colon}` : match,
  );
}

     ```python
         """In a dialogue stimulus, start each later speaker on its own line (matches the database convention)."""
         if not re.match(SPEAKER, s):
             return s
         def brk(m):
             return m.group(1) + (" " if m.group(1) in ("Mr.", "Ms.", "Mrs.", "Dr.") else "\n")
         return re.sub(r"(\S*[.?!\u201d\"])\s+(?=" + SPEAKER + ")", brk, s)
     ```

### What the best ones do

- **They predict the rule and put the conclusion's judgment on the right side.** They write "If [evidence fact], then [conclusion judgment]", often at two levels of abstraction (PT146-S1-Q1, PT155-S4-Q9). When there are several premises, they predict one rule per premise (PT150-S3-Q14 does this too; PT138-S3-Q12).
- **They filter by the outcome first, then check the trigger.** Is the conclusion's language on the right side? If not, the choice is out. If it is, does the stimulus establish the trigger? (PT154-S2-Q8, PT144-S2-Q23). Their stated rule: "flexible on the trigger, stubborn on the outcome" (PT154-S2-Q8, PT101-S2-Q9).
- **When they see pros and cons, they switch to weighing tradeoffs.** They name the upside and the downside, then predict "[the side the author picks] matters more than [the other]". They also explain why an answer with no "should" in it can still win (PT107-S4-Q7, PT108-S2-Q24, PT147-S1-Q14, golden PT138-S3-Q1).
- **They translate conditional wording before judging it.** "Only if" and "only" go on the right; "unless" means "if not"; "if and only if" is a biconditional; negating an AND gives an OR. Then they show that the correct answer is often written in contrapositive form to hide it (PT103-S2-Q23, PT150-S2-Q5, PT144-S3-Q23, PT138-S3-Q12).
- **They give the most-picked trap the longest note and say why it tempts.** Examples: PT144-S3-Q23 B at 30% (affected is not opposed; many years is not never), PT137-S3-Q9 D at 22% (a confiscation rule is not an admissibility rule), PT138-S3-Q12 D at 24% (relative vs absolute), PT144-S2-Q23 D at 36% (relevance is not justification).
- **When the principle is in the stimulus, they say the application already concludes the rule's right side, so the job is to establish the missing trigger** (PT137-S4-Q8, golden PT138-S2-Q5, PT103-S2-Q23).
- **They check what kind of conclusion is being proved.** A consistency claim (PT112-S3-Q20), a comparison (PT151-S3-Q6), a conditional conclusion (PT108-S2-Q24) or an intermediate conclusion (PT155-S4-Q9) each shape what the rule must output.
- **They use one concrete example that carries the logic.** Examples: the Al Capone diary handed over by his daughter (PT137-S3-Q9), frozen broccoli (PT138-S3-Q12), the fisherman scene (PT155-S1-Q16), "Eric is a jerk" (PT108-S2-Q24).
- **They are honest when the key is imperfect.** They say what is off and why it still beats the others (PT148-S1-Q4, PT153-S3-Q2 "only wins because all the other answers lose", PT148-S4-Q8 "affirms a Necessary Assumption").

### What the weaker candidates got wrong

- **Pasted verdict notes.** PT144-S2-Q14 and PT137-S2-Q8 give A through D the identical sentence ("doesn't contain any language like..."). PT145-S2-Q21 has a superb Evaluate on "not X or Y" but pastes B through E.
- **Incomplete notes.** PT150-S2-Q16's E note only diagrams the argument and never tests E. PT153-S3-Q2's E note stops after one sentence.
- **Popular traps under-served.** In PT113-S2-Q22, A drew 18% and C drew 28%, but each gets the same short "wrong topic" treatment as the 3% answers. In PT148-S4-Q8, the note calls D "by far the most attractive" at 6% while C at 16% gets a brief note.
- **Tone and outside facts.** PT149-S4-Q21 opens by mocking the stimulus. PT116-S2-Q21 supports the key with an outside generalization about who becomes close friends. PT107-S4-Q7 brings in genetics that the stimulus never states.
- **Choice notes that describe the wrong choice** (see fidelity, PT101-S2-Q25).

### Fidelity problems found

- **PT101-S2-Q25 (disqualify):** The C note diagrams a trigger about "a hardship greater than the gain they were anticipating", but printed C says "expect that most people will accept the claim as true". ## PT142-S1-Q1 | Most Strongly Supported | C

> Children should be discouraged from reading Jones’s books. Reading them is like eating candy, which provides intense, short-term sensory stimulation but leaves one poorly nourished and dulls one’s taste for better fare. In other words, the problem with letting children read Jones’s books is that _______.
>
> Which one of the following most logically completes the argument above?
>
> (A) it will lead them to develop a taste for candy and sweets
> (B) too many children may become frustrated by their difficulty and stop reading altogether
> (C) their doing so interferes with the development of appreciation for more challenging literature
> (D) their message may undermine the positive teaching done by parents
> (E) children may become so enthralled with books that they will want to spend all their time reading

### Argument Breakdown

**Statements:** Children shouldn't read Jones's books. Reading them is like eating candy: a strong, quick thrill that leaves you poorly nourished and dulls your taste for better food.

**Evaluate:** The blank starts "In other words", so it restates the analogy in plain terms. Map each piece: candy = Jones's books, poor nourishment = not much to gain, a dulled taste for better fare = less appetite for better books.

**Goal:** Reading Jones dulls children's taste for better books.

> (D) Dudley has worked part-time for the company for the past seven years. He applied for parental leave over three months before the birth of his child, so it should be granted to him.
> (E) Maria has worked full-time for the company for the past two years and applied for parental leave six months prior to her adoption of a child, so she should be granted parental leave.

### Argument Breakdown

**Rule:** An eligible employee gets up to six weeks of paid leave. Eligible means applying at least three months before the leave starts *and* having at least one year of full-time employment when applying.

**Evaluate:** Check each person against both requirements, measured at the time of application. Also watch for reasons to deny that the policy never gives.

**Goal:** Someone who meets both requirements and is granted leave.

### Choice Notes

**(A) Violates Rule.** Mac has one year now, but he applied three months ago, when he had only nine months. He wasn't eligible when he applied.

**(B) Violates Rule.** Sara meets both requirements. A recent leave of absence isn't a reason the policy recognizes.

**(C) Violates Rule.** The policy grants "up to" six weeks, so wanting only two is fine. Denying Hal on that basis doesn't follow the policy.

**(D) Violates Rule.** Dudley has worked part-time. The policy requires full-time.

**(E) Correct.** Maria has two years full-time and applied six months ahead. She meets both requirements, so she gets the leave.

The problems also did happen, so the employee's claims aren't false.\n\n**(E) Not Clear.** This is the most-picked trap, at 10%. Promoting a relative over someone else is only partial if the relative wasn't the better choice. E gives no comparison. The relative may well have earned it. A, by contrast, tells us the relatives were the better choice.\n\n## PT115-S4-Q24 | Principle-Conform | E\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Situation:** Raising a park's user fees drives some people away. Fewer users means less wear, so maintenance improves. This holds even if so many people leave that the money for maintenance actually drops.\n\n**Evaluate:** The chain is: raise the fee, lose users, less wear, better condition. The twist is in the last clause. The condition improves even though the money for upkeep goes down. Less use matters more than less money.\n\n**Goal:** A fee increase that drives users away, so the thing ends up in better shape despite less money for its upkeep.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Different Chain.** Better warranties raise market share and cut profits. No fee drives users away, and nothing is wearing out less.\n\n**(B) Different Chain.** The store closes overnight, not raising a fee, and its revenue rises. In the stimulus, revenue can fall while the condition improves.\n\n**(C) Opposite.** Here more money comes in, and the service still gets worse. That reverses the stimulus, where less money and better condition go together.\n\n**(D) Different Chain.** More spending brings more visitors, and the extra revenue covers the cost. Usage goes up, not down.\n\n**(E) Correct.** Library fees rise, there are fewer patrons, and the books are in better repair even though the money for repairs has dropped. Every link matches, including the twist that less money still means better condition.\n\n## PT116-S3-Q3 | Principle-Conform | B\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Situation:** Two equally skilled groups of tennis players. One was told only their rackets were being assessed. The other was told their talent was being measured. The first group played much better.\n\n**Evaluate:** The groups are matched on skill, so the only difference is what they believed was being judged. When players thought their own ability was on the line, they played worse.\n\n**Goal:** People perform better when they don't think their abilities are being judged.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Not the Difference.** This is the trap, picked by 8%. It sounds right, since being watched can make people nervous. But both groups were being watched. What differed was what the players thought was being evaluated: the racket or themselves.\n\n**(B) Correct.** The group that thought only the racket was being judged did better. That's people performing better when they don't believe their abilities are being judged.\n\n**(C) Not Described.** Both groups were equally skilled, and nothing tells us anyone's confidence.\n\n**(D) Not Described.** Nobody here assesses their own talent.\n\n**(E) Not Described.** Nobody is trying to please the testers. E also predicts more effort, while the stimulus is about how well people played.\n\n## PT116-S3-Q5 | Principle-Conform | E\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Rule:** A work of art's aesthetic value lies in its ability to make the audience's experience stimulating.\n\n**Evaluate:** The rule ties value to one thing: the effect on the audience. A judgment conforms if it praises or faults a work because of how it affects its audience. A judgment that rests on the artist, the material, or originality uses some other standard.\n\n**Goal:** A judgment of a work's value based on its effect on the audience.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Wrong Standard.** Being a copy is about originality. An exact copy could still give an audience a stimulating experience.\n\n**(B) Opposite.** The symphony doesn't excite the audience, yet it's called beautiful because it's performed competently. By the critic's standard, failing to stimulate is the problem.\n\n**(C) Wrong Standard.** The cube is praised for a rare material. That says nothing about the audience's experience.\n\n**(D) Wrong Standard.** This is the trap, picked by 6%. A controversial artist might seem stimulating. But D praises the painting for who painted it, not for what it does to the people looking at it.\n\n**(E) Correct.** The poem is called deficient because it has little impact on its audience. Little impact means no stimulating experience. That's exactly what the critic's principle uses to judge value.\n\n## PT117-S3-Q3 | Principle-Conform | D\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** The board shouldn't let the foreign incentives entice it into expanding there without further consideration.\n\n**Evidence:** Expanding could raise profits, but neither country is politically stable.\n\n**Evaluate:** Look at how modest the conclusion is. The chairperson doesn't say \"don't expand.\" They say \"don't jump in without thinking it over.\" Instability is a reason for caution, weighed against the chance at profit. A principle that forbids expansion or ranks stability above everything is stronger than this argument.\n\n**Goal:** Be cautious about expanding into politically unstable countries.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Too Strong.** This is the trap, picked by 11%. \"Never expand\" would settle the matter, but the chairperson only asks for further consideration. That leaves room to expand after all. A rule that forbids expansion outright goes further than the reasoning does.\n\n**(B) Opposite.** This pushes toward expanding wherever there's profit. The chairperson is putting on the brakes.\n\n**(C) Too Strong.** This is the second trap, at 6%. The chairperson raises stability as a concern but never ranks it as the most important factor. They even acknowledge the profit opportunity.\n\n**(D) Correct.** \"Be cautious\" matches \"not without further consideration,\" and \"politically unstable countries\" matches the evidence. This is the principle at exactly the argument's strength.\n\n**(E) Too Strong.** The chairperson says not to let incentives alone entice the board. That isn't the same as always ignoring incentives.\n\n## PT117-S4-Q4 | Principle | A\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Be wary of proposals for radical solutions that are reactions to new statistics.\n\n**Evidence:** A sudden statistical jump in a problem often just reflects greater awareness of the problem or better recording of it.\n\n**Evaluate:** The argument doesn't deny the problem exists. It says the jump in the numbers may come from us noticing more, not from the problem getting worse. If only our awareness has changed, that's no reason for a radical response. The principle connects those ideas.\n\n**Goal:** Greater awareness of a problem doesn't by itself justify a radical solution.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.** \"Better cognizance\" is the heightened awareness from the evidence. \"Does not warrant a radical solution\" is the wariness in the conclusion. If the statistics only show better cognizance, A tells us not to go radical.\n\n**(B) Wrong Doubt.** This is the trap, picked by 10%. It sounds cautious in the same way. But the argument never doubts that the problem exists. It doubts that the problem has suddenly grown. B also covers any attempt to stop a problem, not radical ones.\n\n**(C) Opposite.** The argument is wary of solutions driven by new statistics. Basing them on statistics alone is the reverse.\n\n**(D) Not Described.** Nobody is manipulating the data. The numbers can be completely accurate and still reflect awareness more than a real increase.\n\n**(E) Different Reason.** Radical solutions might backfire, but that isn't the argument's reason for caution. Its reason is that the statistics may not mean what they seem to.\n\n## PT117-S4-Q13 | Principle | D\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Engineers usually stay calm when their work is evaluated, while artists tend to get anxious.\n\n**Evidence:** Anyone can see whether a machine works. Recognizing excellence in art takes rare, subtle perception.\n\n**Evaluate:** The argument explains a difference in anxiety by a difference in how easy the work is to judge. Easy to judge, calm creator. Hard to judge, anxious creator. The principle should be general: about people who create things, not just engineers and artists.\n\n**Goal:** People whose work's success is easy to see worry less about evaluations than people whose work's value is hard to see.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Not the Reasoning.** The argument puts the anxiety down to the work being hard to judge, not to anyone's personality. A makes a claim about personalities that the argument never makes.\n\n**(B) Wrong Subject.** This is the trap, picked by 5%. It mentions the creators' feelings, so it sounds close. But it says a work's value depends on those feelings. The argument says the creators' feelings depend on how easily the work can be judged. B reverses which one depends on which.\n\n**(C) Not Described.** The argument explains why artists get anxious. It never says how engineers or artists should be evaluated.\n\n**(D) Correct.** Machines are things whose success is easily ascertained, and art is something whose value isn't. Engineers worry less and artists worry more. D is the stimulus stated in general terms.\n\n**(E) Wrong Comparison.** The argument compares two kinds of creators. E compares a creator to the evaluators. The stimulus never says how confident evaluators are.\n\n## PT118-S1-Q9 | Principle-Conform | E\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Saying Fits.** Fatima knows enough mathematics to see how much will stay unsolved. That's the saying in action: you need to know a lot before you see how little you know. The story illustrates it, so the phrase is used properly.\n\n**(B) Saying Fits.** Harold has done the same thing many times before. That's selfishness as predictable as gravity, so the quote matches the story. The friends' surprise doesn't change that Harold's behavior was calculable.\n\n**(C) Saying Fits.** Roger won't spend the money because he's frugal. \"A penny saved is a penny earned\" is the frugal person's motto. The story illustrates it.\n\n**(D) Saying Fits.** Sharon loves cats, and her husband, allergic as he is, still sometimes joins her at cat shows. Sharing her life means sharing what she loves, at least a little. The story illustrates the saying.\n\n**(E) Correct.** Raoul's trip ended with a broken leg and two weeks in the hospital. That didn't end well, so \"All's well that ends well\" has no illustration here. The story is an apparent counterexample, and putting \"as the saying goes\" after it is the misuse the principle describes.\n\n## PT118-S3-Q8 | Principle-PSA | C\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Opposite.** The Development Commission insists Figoria has the right to govern its own resources. Handing regulation to an international agreement takes that right away. A works against the commission it is supposed to help.\n\n**(B) Opposite.** If future generations' right to wildlife outranks a nation's economic needs, the Development Commission's appeal to growth loses. That's the Wildlife Commission's side.\n\n**(C) Correct.** Regulate only after commercial development has actually been found to reduce endangered species. The Development Commission says Figoria has conserved, and its development \"might not affect wildlife.\" So no such harm has been found, and regulation isn't justified yet. The Wildlife Commission wants regulation before any harm, which this principle rules out.\n\n**(D) Opposite.** This is the trap, picked by 12%. It talks about how different nations have harmed the environment to different degrees. That's the Development Commission's theme, so it feels like their answer. But read what it concludes: regulation cannot allow for those differences. The commission's whole complaint is that Figoria's record of conserving should count. D says it doesn't.\n\n**(E) Opposite.** If further depletion is imprudent, developing the wetlands is imprudent. That supports the Wildlife Commission.\n\n## PT118-S4-Q2 | Principle-Conform | B\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** The factory shouldn't be required to clean up the wetlands.\n\n**Evidence:** The factory's wastewater polluted the wetlands, but an independent contractor handles all the disposal.\n\n**Evaluate:** The factory admits its wastewater caused the pollution. Its defense is that someone else, acting independently, made the decisions about disposal. The principle: you aren't responsible for harm when an independent party made the choices that caused it.\n\n**Goal:** Someone shouldn't be held responsible for what a separate, independent agent freely did.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Different Reasoning.** This concludes that parents should check teachers' qualifications. Nobody is trying to avoid responsibility.\n\n**(B) Correct.** Parents shouldn't answer for older adolescents, because those adolescents have minds of their own and freely choose what to do. That's the factory's defense: we didn't make the choice, an independent party did.\n\n**(C) Different Reasoning.** This is the trap, picked by 8%. It objects to a burden, as the factory does. But the students' reason is that the material wasn't covered in class. No independent party made the choice. The structure that matters, blaming someone else's free choice, isn't there.\n\n**(D) Different Reasoning.** The appointee is excluded for a conflict of interest. That's about bias, not shifting responsibility.\n\n**(E) Different Reasoning.** This doubts a claim based on witnesses' reports. Nobody's responsibility is being shifted.\n\n## PT119-S2-Q15 | Principle-Conform | C\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(E) Weak #3 Match.** This is the trap, picked by 8%. Sally's family uses jalapeños often, so #1 roughly fits, and she has gotten used to them, so #2 fits. But #3 needs her to come to like them. All we're told is that she can now eat them without discomfort. Tolerating a food isn't liking it. C ends with George \"very fond\" of pierogis, so it hits all three beats.\n\n## PT119-S3-Q12 | Principle-Conform | C\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Situation:** The company's computer experts choose technology that excites them, even though those choices are expensive, buggy and not the most profitable for the company.\n\n**Evaluate:** The experts are choosing for an organization, and they choose by personal taste instead of by what serves the organization. Both halves have to be there. Someone choosing for a group, and personal enjoyment beating the group's interest.\n\n**Goal:** People who choose for an organization pick what they personally enjoy, not what best serves the organization.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Wrong Contrast.** This is the trap, picked by 7%. Executives favoring people who share their interests looks like personal taste. But the alternative they pass over is \"the most education.\" Nothing says education is what serves the company best. The stimulus contrasts personal taste with the organization's interest, and A contrasts it with education.\n\n**(B) Opposite.** Supermarkets choose for profit. That's choosing in the organization's interest, which the experts failed to do.\n\n**(C) Correct.** Librarians choose for the library, they pick books they enjoy, and they pass over books that serve the community the library is for. Personal taste beats the interest of those they choose for.\n\n**(D) No Organization.** Students choosing their own courses are choosing for themselves. Picking easy courses is a personal tradeoff, not a betrayal of an organization's interest.\n\n**(E) Different Motive.** The executives pick what viewers want, which serves the network's audience. They aren't indulging their own taste.\n\n## PT120-S3-Q22 | Principle-Conform | D\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Rule:** If you don't have enough information for a well-informed decision, don't decide on what you have. Keep seeking information until you can decide well.\n\n**Evaluate:** A conforming choice needs both halves. First, the information on hand is inadequate. Second, the response is to go get more information before deciding. A choice that says \"think harder about what you already have\" or \"give up\" doesn't conform.\n\n**Goal:** Someone with inadequate information who goes and gets more before deciding.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Not the Rule.** This says not to trust one model because conflicting models can't all be right. It never says to keep looking for information before deciding.\n\n**(B) Wrong Fix.** This is a trap, picked by 11%. It warns against deciding on one factor alone. But its fix is to weigh the information you already have more carefully. The rule says that when your information is inadequate, you should go out and get more.\n\n**(C) No Decision.** This is the most-picked trap, at 12%. It sounds like the rule because it urges looking for more information. But the rule is triggered by a specific situation: not enough information to make a decision. C has no decision and says \"always\" look, even when the researcher may know enough. That's a general habit, not this rule.\n\n**(D) Correct.** Personal experience is called an \"inadequate basis,\" which is the trigger. Studying reliability histories from many owners is seeking more information before choosing a car. Both halves are there.\n\n**(E) Opposite.** This has the trigger: not enough information. But then it says to give up and admit the meaning can't be found. The rule says to keep looking.\n"}
