Conclusion / Evidence / Evaluate / Goal for an argument the principle must fit or justify.\n\n## PT121-S4-Q6 | Principle-Conform | A\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Situation:** Early industrial machines replaced many unskilled workers with a few skilled ones, and that saved money. Today managers want technology that replaces highly paid skilled workers with fewer, less-skilled ones.\n\n**Evaluate:** The two examples move in opposite directions on skill. Then it was unskilled to skilled, and now it's skilled to less skilled. So skill isn't the common thread. What's the same in both is fewer workers and lower labor costs. The first example even names the motive: the technology was \"economically attractive.\"\n\n**Goal:** Employers adopt new technology because it cuts labor costs.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.** Both examples swap expensive labor for cheaper labor: many workers for a few, highly paid workers for fewer, less-skilled ones. A names the motive behind both.\n\n**(B) Opposite.** Today's managers want to replace skilled workers with less-skilled ones. That doesn't suggest more education will keep workers competitive.\n\n**(C) Too Strong.** This is the trap, picked by 15%. It picks up the modern example, where skilled workers may be replaced. But the first example shows skilled workers winning, so C can't be illustrated by both examples. And managers are only \"looking for\" this technology. We don't know skilled workers have already lost their advantage.\n\n**(D) Not Described.** Both examples cut the number of workers. Nothing says new jobs make up the difference.\n\n**(E) Not Described.** The passage never mentions heavy industry or says which industries are affected.\n\n## PT122-S1-Q14 | Principle Conform | D\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Rule:** If a lie brings about more good than harm, it is morally permissible.\n\n**Evaluate:** The trigger is a comparison: the good the lie does has to outweigh the harm. A choice conforms only if it gives us enough to know the lie comes out ahead. Choices that check some other condition, like whether the activity is bad or who it affects, don't trigger the rule.\n\n**Goal:** A lie judged permissible because it does more good than harm.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Wrong Trigger.** The condition is that what Marcus does isn't bad. That doesn't tell us whether lying to his parents does more good than harm.\n\n**(B) No Weighing.** Lying to the police about a possible criminal might do plenty of harm. B never weighs good against harm.\n\n**(C) Wrong Trigger.** A lie that affects only yourself can still do more harm than good. Who it affects isn't the test.\n\n**(D) Correct.** The lie helps Thomas and does no harm. Some good and zero harm means more good than harm, so Laila's principle makes it permissible.\n\n**(E) No Weighing.** The lie benefits the people deceived but \"may harm others.\" We can't tell which side is bigger, so the rule isn't triggered.\n\n## PT122-S2-Q3 | Principle Conform | C\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Rule:** Efficient employees ignore unimportant tasks with firm schedules and deadlines. They spend that time on projects that could pay off big for the employer if successful, even when the projects are risky.\n\n**Evaluate:** Two halves. The employee sets aside an unimportant scheduled demand, and puts the time into something that could yield a big reward for the employer. Following a schedule isn't efficiency by this definition, and neither is skipping a deadline for more routine work.\n\n**Goal:** Skipping a routine scheduled obligation to pursue something with a big potential payoff for the employer.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Opposite.** This is meeting a supervisor's deadline, which is the kind of demand efficient employees ignore.\n\n**(B) Wrong Payoff.** This is the trap, picked by 4%. It does ignore a deadline, so half the definition fits. But the time goes to routine correspondence that could wait, not a project with a big reward.\n\n**(C) Correct.** Being on time for a monthly meeting is a routine scheduled demand. An urgent call from a major customer could mean a big reward for the employer. Skipping the first for the second is efficiency as the passage describes it.\n\n**(D) Opposite.** Daily meetings about workloads and schedules are scheduling, not a big-reward project.\n\n**(E) Opposite.** Scheduling tasks around the nearest deadlines is exactly what efficient employees ignore.\n\n## PT122-S4-Q9 | Principle Conform | E\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Marketing herbal tinctures wouldn't produce the result the executive wanted, which is more profit.\n\n**Evidence:** Advisers questioned whether the tinctures work, and a variety of reliable medical publications say they're ineffective.\n\n**Evaluate:** The evidence ends at \"reliable sources say these products don't work.\" The conclusion is about profit. So the principle has to connect reliable authorities calling a product ineffective to the product not being profitable.\n\n**Goal:** If reliable authorities declare a product ineffective, promoting it won't be profitable.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Not the Reasoning.** The executive never asks what makes a publication reliable. The publications are already called reliable.\n\n**(B) Stops Short.** This is the trap, picked by 5%. It takes us from reliable sources to \"the tinctures are ineffective.\" But the executive concludes something about profit, and B says nothing about profit. B also needs a majority of reliable sources, and the executive only consulted \"a variety.\"\n\n**(C) Opposite.** This says consulting publications isn't a reliable basis for predicting profit. That's exactly what the executive did, so C undermines the reasoning.\n\n**(D) Wrong Trigger.** This is about adverse effects. The publications say the tinctures don't work, not that they cause harm.\n\n**(E) Correct.** The trigger is a number of reliable authorities calling the products ineffective, which is the executive's evidence. The outcome is that promoting them won't be profitable, which is the conclusion. E is the whole argument as a rule.\n\n## PT127-S1-Q8 | Principle-Conform | D\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** The company can demand that Ellison stop, but it can't justifiably punish Ellison.\n\n**Evidence:** Ellison admitted the illegal transactions when shown the evidence. But the company got that evidence by illegally recording Ellison's conversations.\n\n**Evaluate:** Ellison is guilty, and the argument doesn't deny it. What blocks punishment is how the evidence came out: the party who wants to punish broke the law to uncover the wrongdoing. The principle: if you discovered someone's wrongdoing through your own illegal act, you can't justifiably punish them for it.\n\n**Goal:** A guilty party who can't be punished because the punisher discovered the wrongdoing illegally.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Wrong Structure.** Long's illegal act is the punishment, stealing back, not the way Price's theft was discovered. Price confessed. Nothing about the discovery was illegal.\n\n**(B) Wrong Reason.** Shakila can't report the secretary because Shakila once did the same thing. That's hypocrisy, not evidence gathered illegally.\n\n**(C) Wrong Person.** Takashi broke curfew on Monday, but the sighting was on Tuesday, so Takashi's violation had nothing to do with discovering Sarah. And Takashi isn't the one punishing. Sarah's parents are, and they did nothing wrong.\n\n**(D) Correct.** The conservation officer found Kuttner's illegal traps while trespassing on Kuttner's land, so the discovery itself was illegal. Kuttner admits it, and the officer, the one who would punish, can't justifiably do so. That matches the company and Ellison.\n\n**(E) Wrong Reason.** The board can't act because it pardoned others before. That's about consistency, and the evidence against Ramirez wasn't obtained illegally.\n\n## PT128-S2-Q14 | Principle Conform | B\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Rule:** It's acceptable not to keep a promise if either (1) the person you promised tells you not to keep it, or (2) circumstances beyond your control make you unable to keep it.\n\n**Evaluate:** The rule only gives conditions for when breaking a promise is acceptable. It never says when breaking one is unacceptable, and it never says when keeping one is unacceptable. So a correct application should conclude \"it was acceptable not to keep it,\" with one of the two conditions met.\n\n**Goal:** A promise broken because the promisee released the promisor or circumstances beyond the promisor's control prevented it, judged acceptable.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Not an Application.** The rule never makes keeping a promise unacceptable, and owing Maria money isn't one of its conditions.\n\n**(B) Correct.** Alan was hurt and couldn't come, so Felicia couldn't tutor Alan that Tuesday. That's a circumstance beyond Felicia's control, condition 2, and the conclusion is that not tutoring was acceptable.\n\n**(C) Not an Application.** Owen asked to change the day. The rule says nothing about having to agree to a new request, and it never concludes that anything is unacceptable.\n\n**(D) Contradicts the Rule.** Without the keys, Quinn couldn't get in. That's a circumstance beyond Quinn's control, so condition 2 makes not watering acceptable. D only checks condition 1 and reaches the opposite verdict.\n\n**(E) Misapplies the Rule.** Ian was unable to make it, but only because Ian chose to return library books first. That was within Ian's control, so condition 2 doesn't apply, and nobody released Ian either.\n\n## PT132-S4-Q20 | Principle-Strengthen | E\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** The manufacturer's earlier ignorance doesn't free it from all responsibility for the workers' illnesses.\n\n**Evidence:** Substance T caused at least some of the illnesses. If the manufacturer had investigated T's safety before exposing workers, many of those illnesses would have been prevented.\n\n**Evaluate:** The key evidence is that the harm was preventable. The conclusion is that the manufacturer bears some responsibility. So the rule needs \"preventable\" on the left and \"responsible\" on the right: if a manufacturer's action harms people and the harm was preventable, the manufacturer is responsible.\n\n**Goal:** Manufacturers are responsible for preventable harmful consequences of their actions.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Wrong Conclusion.** This says harmed employees should be compensated. It doesn't say who is responsible, so it doesn't reach the manufacturer.\n\n**(B) Wrong Direction.** \"Only\" puts preventable on the right: responsible → preventable. That tells us when a manufacturer is not responsible, when the harm couldn't be prevented. It can't prove the manufacturer is responsible. Knowing the harm was preventable doesn't trigger anything.\n\n**(C) Wrong Trigger.** This covers risks the manufacturer was aware of. Here it was ignorant, so C never applies.\n\n**(D) Opposite.** If preventability is irrelevant, the argument's main evidence counts for nothing.\n\n**(E) Correct.** The workers are innocent people harmed by T, and the evidence says the illnesses were preventable. Both conditions are met, so the manufacturer is held responsible. That's the conclusion.\n\n## PT142-S1-Q3 | Principle-Conform | B\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** The government shouldn't fund any part of its health services with lottery revenue.\n\n**Evidence:** The health services are essential, and lottery revenue could decline, leaving a budget shortfall.\n\n**Evaluate:** Two facts lead to the conclusion. These services are essential, and lottery money is unreliable. The principle puts them together: essential services need reliable funding. Lottery money isn't reliable, so none of it should pay for them.\n\n**Goal:** Essential services should be funded only from reliable sources.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Not the Reasoning.** The editorial never compares spending on essential and nonessential services.\n\n**(B) Correct.** The health services are essential, so they must be funded from reliable sources. Lottery revenue could decline, so it isn't reliable. That rules out using lottery money for any part of them, which is the conclusion.\n\n**(C) Too Weak.** This bans being \"entirely\" dependent on lottery money. The editorial bans funding \"any part\" of the services that way. Under C, partial lottery funding would be fine.\n\n**(D) Not the Reasoning.** The editorial says these health services are essential. It doesn't say every health service must be treated that way.\n\n**(E) Different Remedy.** This saves lottery money for future shortfalls. The editorial's answer is to stop relying on lottery money for these services at all.\n\n## PT143-S1-Q2 | Principle-Conform | C\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Popular science publications should give up trying to explain new science to a wide audience.\n\n**Evidence:** To reach a wide audience, they have to rely on metaphor, which usually gets the science wrong. If they write more rigorously, they get the science right but lose the wide audience.\n\n**Evaluate:** This is a tradeoff with two options. Reach a wide audience and be inaccurate, or be accurate and reach fewer people. The author picks accuracy. Nothing in the evidence says which matters more. That ranking is what the principle has to supply.\n\n**Goal:** Being accurate matters more than reaching a wide audience.\n\n## PT143-S3-Q3 | Principle-Strengthen | C\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Dismissing McBride's complaint would be unfair.\n\n**Evidence:** The rules call for Form 283, but Bureau staff gave McBride Form 5. McBride used it intending to file a formal complaint.\n\n**Evaluate:** The wrong form came from the government agency, not from McBride. McBride did what the staff said. The principle needs to connect \"the mistake was the agency's\" to \"dismissing the complaint is unfair.\"\n\n**Goal:** It's unfair to dismiss someone's complaint because of a government agency's mistake.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Wrong Outcome.** This says people should be told the regulations. Even if McBride should have been told, A doesn't say anything about whether dismissal would be unfair.\n\n**(B) Wrong Problem.** The issue isn't that Form 5 was hard to fill out. It's that it was the wrong form. And B says nothing about dismissal.\n\n**(C) Correct.** The incorrect action was the Bureau staff handing over Form 5, and the Bureau is a government agency. So dismissing the complaint for that reason is unfair. That's the conclusion.\n\n**(D) Not Shown.** We know staff handed out the wrong form, not that the procedures are too complex for them. And D tells agencies how to design procedures. It doesn't say dismissing the complaint is unfair.\n\n**(E) Wrong Side.** This protects the nightclub. Nothing says the nightclub lacked a chance to defend itself, and the conclusion is about fairness to McBride.\n\n## PT144-S2-Q6 | Principle-Strengthen | D\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** The victim surcharge is unfair to nonviolent criminals.\n\n**Evidence:** The surcharge funds services for victims of violent crimes, but it applies to every crime, including nonviolent ones like petty theft.\n\n**Evaluate:** The lawyer's complaint is a mismatch. Someone convicted of petty theft pays for services for victims of violent crime, a more serious kind of crime than theirs. The principle has to say that's not a fair thing to make a criminal pay for.\n\n**Goal:** Criminals shouldn't have to pay for services for victims of crimes more serious than their own.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Not the Reasoning.** Deterrence never comes up. The lawyer's objection is about who pays for what.\n\n**(B) Doesn't Reach.** This compares overall penalties. The surcharge is added \"in addition to any other penalties\", so violent criminals may still pay more overall. B doesn't make the surcharge unfair.\n\n**(C) Not Shown.** Nothing suggests the money is spent on anything other than services. The lawyer's complaint is who pays, not where the money goes.\n\n**(D) Correct.** A petty thief pays for services for victims of violent crime, which is more serious than petty theft. D says that criminal shouldn't have to pay, so the surcharge is unfair to nonviolent criminals.\n\n**(E) Out of Scope.** Fines for theft based on the value stolen have nothing to do with the victim surcharge.\n\n## PT144-S4-Q11 | Principle-Conform | B\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Rule:** Two rules. (1) Someone who knowingly brings about misfortune should be blamed. (2) Someone who unwittingly brings about misfortune that they couldn't reasonably have foreseen should never be blamed.\n\n**Evaluate:** Notice the gap. If someone acted unwittingly but could have foreseen the misfortune, neither rule applies. Rule 1 needs knowledge, and rule 2 needs it to be unforeseeable. So the rules can only justify blaming a knowing actor, or not blaming an unwitting actor who couldn't have foreseen it.\n\n**Goal:** Someone unaware of the risk, who couldn't reasonably have foreseen it, shouldn't be blamed.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Rule Not Triggered.** Riley would have realized it with a moment's thought, so the accident was foreseeable. Rule 2 doesn't apply, and no rule says Riley escapes blame.\n\n**(B) Correct.** Oblicek had no idea the loan could bankrupt the business and couldn't reasonably have foreseen it. That's rule 2 exactly: unwitting and unforeseeable, so Oblicek should not be blamed.\n\n**(C) Rule Not Triggered.** Gougon worried the sauce might make people sick but had no reason to think it would. Worry isn't knowledge, so rule 1 doesn't apply. No rule says Gougon should be blamed.\n\n**(D) Rule Not Triggered.** The rules never say who is the only one to blame. And Dr. Fitzpatrick acted unknowingly, so rule 1 doesn't make the doctor blameworthy.\n\n**(E) Rule Not Triggered.** This is the tempting one. Kapp should have seen the fire coming, and blaming Kapp feels right. But Kapp didn't realize it, so rule 1 (knowingly) doesn't apply. Rule 2 only excuses. No rule here blames someone who was unwitting but should have known.\n\n## PT145-S4-Q1 | Principle-Strengthen | A\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Grenier almost certainly won't be elected mayor.\n\n**Evidence:** Grenier recently argued against raising city employees' wages and now supports it. Grenier's explanation, sincere as it is, won't matter, because most voters will see Grenier as insincere.\n\n**Evaluate:** The evidence ends with voters seeing Grenier as insincere. The conclusion is that Grenier loses. The missing link: voters don't vote for politicians they think are insincere.\n\n**Goal:** Voters are unlikely to vote for a politician they see as insincere.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.** Most voters will see Grenier as insincere, and A says voters are unlikely to vote for such a politician. That leads straight to Grenier losing.\n\n**(B) Opposite.** If voters don't notice changes in stance, the flip-flop wouldn't hurt Grenier. The pundit says voters will notice and react.\n\n**(C) Opposite.** If voters agree with Grenier's current position on wages, this says the old views won't matter. That would help Grenier.\n\n**(D) Not the Reasoning.** The pundit's reasoning is about sincerity, not whether voters think Grenier understands their finances.\n\n**(E) Wrong Trigger.** The voters doubt Grenier because the stance changed, not because Grenier's beliefs differ from theirs. And E only predicts doubt. It doesn't get us to losing the election.\n\n## PT156-S2-Q12 | Principle-Strengthen | C\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** The current air quality standards, already quite stringent, should not be raised.\n\n**Evidence:** Tighter standards would drive industries to places with looser rules. There isn't enough evidence that the reduced pollution would make up for the lost jobs.\n\n**Evaluate:** The politician admits raising the standards would reduce pollution. The argument isn't \"raising them is bad.\" It's \"we don't have enough evidence that raising them is better.\" So the principle has to say a policy shouldn't change without good evidence that the change is better.\n\n**Goal:** Don't change a policy unless there's strong evidence the change leads to better results.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Not the Reasoning.** Protecting key industries leans the politician's way. But the argument turns on missing evidence about whether the change is worth it. A ignores that and never weighs the pollution benefit the politician admits.\n\n**(B) Out of Scope.** Public acceptance never comes up.\n\n**(C) Correct.** \"Altered only if\" puts compelling evidence on the right: change → compelling evidence. Contrapose it: no compelling evidence → don't change. The politician says the evidence isn't there, so the standards shouldn't be raised.\n\n**(D) Opposite.** Both options here have upsides and downsides: cleaner air on one side, jobs on the other. D says that's when policy should be changed, which is the reverse of the conclusion.\n\n**(E) Opposite.** The politician lacks clear evidence that the benefits would make up for the losses. E says to assume they would, which supports raising the standards.\n\n## PT156-S4-Q26 | Principle-Strengthen | C\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Nuclear power advocates who call on antinuclear activists to \"live up to their own ideals\" by helping find better ways to dispose of nuclear waste are being dishonest.\n\n**Evidence:** The activists want nuclear power gone as soon as possible. Better waste disposal would probably make nuclear power more acceptable and more likely to continue.\n\n**Evaluate:** The request is presented as serving the activists' ideals, but complying would work against the activists' goal. The conclusion calls that dishonest. The principle has to say that asking people to undermine their own goals in the name of their ideals is dishonest.\n\n**Goal:** It's dishonest to ask people to do something that could undermine their goals for the sake of their ideals.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Wrong Judgment.** This is about irresponsibility. The conclusion is about dishonesty.\n\n**(B) Wrong Judgment.** This supports the activists' preference for eliminating nuclear power. It says nothing about the advocates being dishonest.\n\n**(C) Correct.** Better waste disposal could keep nuclear power going, which undermines the activists' goal. The advocates still ask for it in the name of the activists' ideals. C calls that dishonest, which is the conclusion.\n\n**(D) Wrong Judgment.** This is about irresponsibility, not dishonesty. And the advocates do believe nuclear power is acceptable, so D's trigger isn't met.\n\n**(E) Wrong Trigger.** The advocates' ideals are no secret. The letter's complaint isn't that they hid their views. It's that the request undermines the activists' goals.\n\n## PT159-S1-Q14 | Principle-Strengthen | C\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Before any new genetically engineered crop goes into agricultural production, rigorous safety testing should be required.\n\n**Evidence:** These crops are being adopted fast and monitored loosely, which poses a significant risk to ecosystems. const sharedPassageMetadataPrefixPattern =
  /^\s*(?:The following passage is used for Section\s+\d+,\s+questions\s+\d+\s+through\s+\d+\.|Questions?\s+\d+\s+(?:through|and|[-–])\s+\d+\s+refer to the following passage\.)\s*/i;
const sharedPassageRangePattern =
  /^\s*(?:The following passage is used for Section\s+\d+,\s+questions\s+(\d+)\s+through\s+(\d+)\.|Questions?\s+(\d+)\s+(?:through|and|[-–])\s+(\d+)\s+refer to the following passage\.)\s*/i;

function stripSharedPassageMetadataPrefix(text: string): string {
  return text.replace(sharedPassageMetadataPrefixPattern, '').trim();
}

function normalizeProseHardWraps(text: string): string {
  return text
    .replace(/\r\n?/g, '\n')
    .split(/\n{2,}/)
    .map((paragraph) => paragraph.replace(/[ \t]*\n[ \t]*/g, ' ').replace(/[ \t]{2,}/g, ' ').trim())
    .filter(Boolean)
    .join('\n\n');
}

function getSharedPassageRange(text: string): { start: number; end: number } | null {
  const match = text.match(sharedPassageRangePattern);
  if (!match) return null;

  if (!Number.isFinite(start) || !Number.isFinite(end) || start > end) return null;

  return { start, end };
}

const dialogueIntroPattern = /^[A-Z][A-Za-z’' -]{1,80}:\s+/;
const dialogueTransitionPattern = /[.!?]["”')\]]?\s+[A-Z][A-Za-z’' -]{1,80}:\s+/;
// Captures: 1) sentence-ending punctuation, 2) the candidate speaker label
// (without its trailing colon/space), 3) the colon + whitespace that follows.
const dialogueTurnBreakPattern =
  /([.!?]["”')\]]?)\s+([A-Z][A-Za-z’' -]{1,80})(:\s+)/g;

function normalizeDialogueSpeakerBreaks(text: string): string {
  if (!dialogueIntroPattern.test(text) || !dialogueTransitionPattern.test(text)) return text;

  return text.replace(dialogueTurnBreakPattern, (match, punct, label, colon) =>
    looksLikeSpeakerLabel(label) ? `${punct}\n\n${label}${colon}` : match,
  );
}

# Session Handoff

Produce a repeatable end-of-session summary so Joshua can `/clear` and start a fresh agent without losing continuity. The next agent should pick up by reading this summary alone.

This is a **context-handoff artifact**, not a status report. The audience is a future instance of you, not a stakeholder.

**Handoff vs. wrapup:** run `session-handoff` when the *context window* is the problem — nearing ~250k tokens (the dumb zone), or passing work between Claude and Codex. It is chat-only and writes nothing. Run `wrapup` when the *work day* is done — it strikes tasks, refreshes `wiki/hot.md`, and appends `wiki/log.md`. They can be run back to back (wrapup to persist, then handoff to reset).

## When to invoke

Joshua says: "session handoff", "hand off", "handoff summary", "summarize before I clear", or any near-equivalent. Note "let's wrap up" belongs to `wrapup`, not here — if he says that and the context window is also deep, run `wrapup` first, then offer this. Also invoke proactively if he says he's about to `/clear` without having run it, or if the session is clearly deep into the dumb zone.

## How to produce the summary

1. **Review the full conversation**, not just the last few turns. Handoffs miss things when they only summarize recent context.
2. **Pull state from these sources (in order):**
   - Plan files referenced this session (check `~/.claude/plans/` if a plan was mentioned).
   - TodoWrite state — any in-progress or pending tasks.
   - Background processes started with `run_in_background` — shell IDs are load-bearing for the next agent.
   - Files created or modified this session — you know what you touched; don't grep to re-discover.
   - Memory files written or updated (`~/.claude/projects/C--Users-Joshu-dev-ai-os/memory/`).
   - Unresolved questions — things you asked Joshua that never got a clear answer, or things he asked that got deflected.
3. **Do NOT audit the filesystem.** This is synthesis of what happened in THIS session. No `git log`, no broad `Glob` sweeps. If you didn't touch it this session, it doesn't belong here.
4. **Produce the output in chat.** Do not write a file. Do not update memory. Chat-only.

## Output template — use exactly this structure, every time

```
# Session Handoff — <one-line title of what this session was about>
```

## Hard rules

1. **Chat output only.** Never write the handoff to a file. Never update memory from this skill. (That is `wrapup`'s job, not this one.)
2. **Never invent state.** If a section has nothing to report, write "none" — do not omit the section. Structure stability is the whole point.
3. **Absolute paths always.** The next agent may have a different working directory, or be Codex.
4. **If a plan file drove the session, name it first** in "Key files" so the next agent reads it before anything else.
5. **No emojis, no hype, no "great job" summaries.** Terse and concrete — paths, commands, shell IDs, decisions. Tone of a seasoned engineer handing off at end-of-shift.
6. **Background process IDs are critical.** If you started any `run_in_background` shells, their IDs must appear in "Running state" with the kill command — the next agent cannot find them otherwise.
7. **Stamp verified state, and separate it from assumed state.** Run `date "+%H:%M"` and use the real time. Every claim about live systems (deploy status, DB contents, what was sent, what is published) is either something you actually checked this session — say how — or explicitly marked NOT re-verified. A handoff that presents stale belief as current state makes the next session re-derive everything, which is the exact cost this skill exists to remove.
8. **Open questions are obligations, not notes.** Anything under OPEN must be resolved by the next session or re-asked to Joshua before it starts new work. Requirements have been silently re-typed across sessions, and a promised artifact once never arrived because nobody re-asked. If a question was open in the handoff you are picking up from, it is the first thing you raise.

## Anti-patterns — do not do these

- Summarizing the last 3 turns and calling it a handoff.
- Listing files by relative path.
- Skipping "Running state" because "nothing is running" — write "none" instead.
- Writing the summary to any file. This is chat-only by design.
- Adding a "what went well / what went poorly" retrospective. This isn't a retro.
- Recommending next steps beyond the single "Pick up here" line. The next agent decides; you just hand off.
